Haruki Murakami’s “Samsa in Love”: A Story of Becoming Human

Mostafa Auvi (মোস্তফা অভি) · 2026-11-25

When one begins reading Haruki Murakami’s Samsa in Love, Kafka’s The Metamorphosis comes to mind almost immediately. Kafka’s Gregor Samsa wakes one morning to discover that he has been transformed into a gigantic insect. Murakami begins from the opposite direction. His Samsa wakes to discover that he has become human. Yet with his new body comes an unfamiliar world. He has no real knowledge of his own body. He cannot walk properly, does not know how to dress, and is puzzled by the sensations of hunger and cold. He must learn from the beginning what it means to live among human beings.

To see this reversal merely as a clever rewriting of Kafka is to miss much of what Murakami is doing. Even after Gregor becomes an insect, he retains his human memories, his sense of duty and his attachment to his family. Gradually, however, his family refuses to recognise him as human. Murakami’s Samsa stands in the opposite position. His body is human, but he has yet to learn the rules of human life. Apart from his name, he knows almost nothing about his identity. He has no memories of the past. He has entered the world in a human body, but human habits, shame, social awareness and the language of affection are all new to him.

This is where the story raises an important question: is a person human simply because of the body he possesses? Or does our humanity take shape through our ability to understand another person’s feelings, form relationships and long for someone who is not ourselves? Samsa’s experience suggests that having a human body and becoming human are not the same thing. He has to learn how to walk, how to eat and how to speak to others. Gradually he discovers that human life contains something beyond hunger and physical need. There is attraction, curiosity and the desire to draw close to another person. Through this desire, his human life begins.

At the beginning of the story, Samsa’s behaviour still carries clear traces of his former existence as an insect. When food is placed before him, he does not think about manners or table etiquette. He eats because he is hungry; food, for him, means survival. He understands clothing mainly as protection from the cold and as a way of covering his body. Somewhere inside him remains the instinct of a vulnerable creature trying to keep itself safe. Even walking is difficult. Standing on two legs does not feel natural. He struggles to keep his balance, fears the stairs and moves by holding on to walls and railings. He is gradually becoming acquainted with his hands, knees, waist and neck. The scenes can be amusing, but beneath the humour there is a persistent uneasiness. The body that we normally accept as our own from birth is, for Samsa, unfamiliar and potentially dangerous.

This is one of the great differences between Murakami’s Samsa and Kafka’s Gregor. Gregor remains tied to the concerns of his former life even after becoming an insect. His inability to go to work, his family’s expenses and the burden of debt continue to trouble him. His body changes, but his mind remains that of the hardworking employee he once was. Murakami’s Samsa, by contrast, has no past behind him. He does not know what he was before, where his family is or how he came to live in this house. He carries no burden of the past. He has only the needs of the present. Kafka’s Gregor becomes isolated from a society he already knows; Murakami’s Samsa enters a society he does not yet understand. One becomes an insect while retaining human memory; the other, almost like an insect without memory, tries to learn how to become human.

In Kafka’s world, it is the family that gradually turns Gregor into an outcast. He can no longer earn money and can no longer communicate, and his human identity is slowly denied. In Murakami’s story, Samsa is human, yet becoming human is difficult even for him. He regards his body as weak and inconvenient. At one point he imagines that perhaps life would be easier if he could remain a fish or a sunflower. But when he becomes attracted to a young woman, he begins to discover a new possibility within the very body that had seemed such a burden. The body that initially brings him discomfort eventually becomes the means through which he experiences the possibility of love.

The story’s most important encounter comes with the arrival of a young, hunchbacked locksmith. She comes to Samsa’s house to repair a lock. At first she appears small, somewhat rough and suspicious. Her back is bent forward, which makes her look shorter than she really is. She raises her head to look at Samsa, turns her body as she speaks, and bends over the lock when she works. Her movements are unlike those of most people. Yet her physical condition has not made her passive or helpless. She knows her trade, understands her responsibilities and has left home to complete a specific job in a dangerous city.

Her roughness should not be mistaken simply for hardness of character. She is suspicious of Samsa’s identity and does not readily believe what he tells her. She asks questions about the house and about the people who live there. There is a kind of vigilance in her behaviour. She is moving through a city where soldiers, tanks, checkpoints and the fear of arrest have entered ordinary life. The men in her family cannot safely go outside. No one knows when a person who leaves home will return, or whether he will return at all. The responsibility of the household has therefore fallen partly upon her. She has crossed the city alone because the work has to be done.

Her instinct for self-protection is unmistakable. As soon as she enters, she studies the surroundings and the person in front of her. She notices Samsa’s clothes and his strange behaviour. She understands that something about the house is not normal, yet she does not abandon her work. Her speech contains irritation and, at times, a touch of sarcasm. When necessary, however, she asks direct questions without hesitation. This can be understood as a form of practical self-defence. In a city where moving about alone as a woman is already dangerous, excessive trust could put her at risk. She therefore keeps a certain psychological distance from the people around her.

Her body is also connected to this instinct for self-protection. She knows that society may judge her by her appearance before it notices her work or her character. Her curved back makes her visibly different. She is aware that some people will attach less importance to her because of it. Yet she has not accepted that difference as a personal weakness. Instead, she has learned to live with the way others look at her and to move through a dangerous city despite it. The cruelty of social judgement contains, paradoxically, a small survival strategy. A body that causes society to overlook her may, under certain circumstances, also help her pass unnoticed.

Yet reducing her to the symbol of a helpless woman would erase much of her personality. She is a skilled professional. Her competence is visible in every stage of the repair. She takes out her tools and arranges them, examines the lock from different angles, looks inside it, checks the mechanism carefully and uses her screwdriver when necessary. She does not work in a state of confusion. When Samsa cannot even properly understand the position of the lock, she becomes irritated, but she does not abandon the job. She continues examining the doors herself. The scene makes her professional confidence clear.

Even with fear and uncertainty spreading through the city, she continues to take her work seriously. Repairing a lock may not solve any great problem in the world. For her, however, it is a real responsibility. She has come to do a job, and she intends to finish it. There is a kind of professional integrity in this. She does not simply abandon her responsibility because danger exists, yet she does not ignore the risks either. Samsa has never understood the meaning of human duty. Now he watches someone so absorbed in her work that the abnormal world around her cannot completely distract her.

The symbolic meaning of the lock is also worth considering. A lock protects a room or a private space. Repairing a lock means restoring a damaged form of security. Yet the house itself seems to exist in a state of insecurity. Wooden boards cover the windows, furniture is scarce, family members have suddenly disappeared, and the rooms feel less like a normal home than a place of confinement. The city outside is also divided by locked doors, checkpoints and military control. In such a world, repairing a lock suggests both private protection and a larger condition of social imprisonment.

The sight of the locksmith at work awakens a new kind of attraction in Samsa. He notices how she bends while working, how she turns her body, how she reaches for a tool and then straightens again. Her movements seem strange to him, yet they also fascinate him. Samsa is himself learning how to inhabit a human body. It is therefore natural that the physical language of another person should become an object of intense curiosity. He observes her gestures without understanding their social or personal meaning. He does not know which gesture expresses irritation, which indicates embarrassment, which means refusal and which is simply part of ordinary movement. To him, the human body is a new language whose alphabet he has only begun to learn.

Here Murakami treats physical attraction in a particularly complicated way. When the young woman is absorbed in her work, Samsa feels a new kind of excitement. He does not understand what it means. The connection between bodily response and emotional feeling is still unknown to him. Sexual attraction is an ordinary part of human life, but for Samsa it is new and bewildering. He is fascinated by the woman’s skill and by the movements of her body, while at the same time finding himself unable to fully understand his own physical response. The experience takes him another step towards becoming human because, for the first time, he feels a personal desire directed towards another person.

Yet one thing must be kept in mind: Samsa’s attraction is not necessarily the woman’s own feeling. Samsa is fascinated by her, but she does not initially look at him in the same way. She is suspicious of him, irritated by his ignorance and focused on completing her work. His attraction is therefore largely one-sided and immature. He wants to know her, but he is also curious about her body and wants to touch it. His feelings cannot be described as a simple, equal or mature relationship. They belong to someone who is experiencing desire for the first time and has not yet learned to understand another person’s independence or the limits of his own emotions.

Murakami’s description of the woman’s body also brings together difference and beauty. By conventional standards, she might not be considered conventionally attractive. Her back is curved and her movements are unusual. Yet, through Samsa’s eyes, precisely this difference becomes part of her attraction. He does not pity her. Instead, he finds a kind of natural rhythm in the way she moves. Samsa himself struggles to walk on two legs, and the woman’s curved way of moving seems, to him, almost easier and more natural. A body that society calls abnormal begins to appear perfectly logical when seen through unfamiliar eyes. This is one of Murakami’s quieter techniques.

In this context, Samsa compares the woman’s walk to the movement of an insect. He remembers a creature that moves quickly across the surface of water. The comparison reveals the lingering shadow of his own animal past. He is now human, yet the memory of another kind of life remains in the way he sees the world. Human walking seems difficult to him, while the bent movement of the young woman feels almost instinctive. Murakami thereby asks whether the human body is always the most natural form. Every body has its own rhythm, limitations and ways of finding balance.

For this reason, Samsa’s attraction to the young woman cannot be reduced to sexual desire alone. It contains curiosity, wonder, a degree of empathy and the first experience of accepting another body in its difference. Yet this acceptance is not fully conscious or ethically developed. Samsa is still learning. He sees the woman’s body, but he has not yet learned to understand the person within it. His incompleteness makes him convincing. At the beginning of his human life, his desire is both innocent and slightly self-centred.

Another important aspect of the woman’s behaviour is the combination of professional commitment and limited sympathy towards Samsa. She becomes irritated when he reveals his ignorance, but she does not simply insult him and leave. Even after discovering that the people of the house are absent, she attempts to finish her work. When she notices Samsa’s difficulty in walking, she asks why he is having such trouble. Her words may be hard, but she is not indifferent to another human being. This duality prevents her from becoming a one-dimensional character. She has learned to be hard in order to survive, yet she still possesses a capacity for tenderness.

The city makes their relationship even more complicated. The city is Prague, but Murakami does not present Prague through its historical beauty or architecture. His Prague is a city of soldiers, tanks, checkpoints, arrests and fear. Moving through the streets is dangerous. No one knows who may be taken away or when. The men in the woman’s family are afraid to go outside. She is sent out alone partly because her family believes that her physical appearance may make her less conspicuous or less threatening in the eyes of the soldiers. Political circumstances therefore enter directly into private life, family responsibility and freedom of movement.

There is a clear contrast between the inside and outside worlds. Inside, Samsa is occupied with his body, his hunger, his clothing and his emerging desire. Outside, military operations and repression are taking place. At first he understands none of it. Words such as soldiers, tanks and arrests mean little to him. Through the young woman, he begins to learn that the world around him is breaking apart. The knowledge is frightening, yet he does not respond to it with an immediate political consciousness. His attention remains fixed on his fascination with her. Murakami shows that even in the middle of a large political catastrophe, private feelings can still emerge. War can control human lives, but it cannot completely erase desire.

The instability of the city is more than background; it helps explain the characters’ behaviour. The woman’s roughness, her determination to finish the job quickly, the inability of the men in her family to go outside, her solitary movements through the city—all carry the mark of the political situation. The wooden boards over Samsa’s window and the emptiness of the house belong to the same atmosphere of fear. The house seems to have hidden itself from the dangers outside, yet the hiding place offers no real security. The need to repair the lock becomes another small sign of this larger insecurity.

Kafka’s story also deals with social confinement. Yet in his world the pressure is more bureaucratic, familial and existential. Gregor’s office, his debts and his family’s dependence on his income form an invisible prison. His transformation into an insect makes that prison visible. Murakami places a similar condition of confinement within a more openly political and military environment. Both stories are concerned with isolation, but the causes and forms of that isolation differ. Kafka’s Gregor becomes an outcast within his own family. Murakami’s Samsa has not yet even reached the stage of belonging to a family or society.

The role of family is also very different in the two stories. Kafka’s family initially tries to adapt to Gregor’s transformation, but eventually begins to regard him as a burden. His sister’s changing attitude, in particular, accelerates his social death. In Murakami’s story, Samsa’s family is absent. We do not know where they have gone, why they have left or whether they will ever return. The family exists as a mystery created by absence. Samsa knows nothing about them, yet he lives in their house. Their absence deepens the emptiness at the centre of his identity.

Memory and language are equally important. Samsa knows his name and has some sense that certain social behaviours are expected of him, but many words and ideas remain unclear. His language is developing as he moves through the world. He can speak, yet uncertainty often enters his speech. He cannot always give a clear answer to a simple question. The young woman becomes irritated by this because language is not merely a means of communication; it is also a condition of entering society. Samsa must learn both human language and the rules of conversation.

The difference becomes even clearer in his conversations with the locksmith. She understands the practical world, knows why she is there and understands the language of danger. Samsa understands none of this. Yet after meeting her, he begins to think about the future for the first time. He wants to see her again. He wants to speak to her. He wants to understand the mysteries of the world. These desires are different from hunger or the need to escape the cold. They are desires for connection. Samsa no longer wants to remain trapped inside his own body. He wants to reach another human being.

This is why the story’s treatment of love matters. Murakami does not present love as the result of a mature relationship, mutual commitment or a long acquaintance. Samsa has seen the young woman only briefly. They have barely spoken. Yet the encounter changes the direction of his life. Before meeting her, he imagines that perhaps it would be easier to remain a fish or a sunflower because the human body is so troublesome. After meeting her, he understands that without being human he could not experience what he is now feeling. He becomes willing to accept the difficulties of the human body because that body has given him the possibility of loving another person.

The woman’s departure makes this transformation visible. She must return through the dangerous city, where soldiers, tanks and the possibility of arrest await her. She nevertheless finishes her work and leaves. Samsa expresses his desire to see her again. She offers no direct promise, but there is a small warmth in her final words. To Samsa, that warmth becomes significant. For the first time he learns that even a small gesture of kindness from another person can alter the meaning of life.

His decision, towards the end of the story, to learn how to dress himself properly is therefore meaningful. At first clothing is simply a way of protecting himself from the cold. Later he begins to understand that clothing also carries a social meaning. He wants to prepare himself. The coming day is not merely another day; it is a step towards entering the human world. He still does not know how to walk properly, how to speak properly or how to understand another person. But he is now willing to learn.

In Murakami’s story, the hunchbacked locksmith therefore does more than initiate Samsa’s first experience of love. She gives him his first practical lesson in the human world. Her professional competence introduces him to the idea of responsibility. Her caution teaches him that society can be dangerous. Her physical movements introduce him to the diversity of human bodies. And her small gesture of kindness awakens in him the desire for connection. She herself may never realise how important she has become to Samsa. Yet her presence gives meaning to his transformation.

At the same time, it would be a mistake to turn her entirely into a symbol. She is a young woman living with concrete needs. She has a family, a profession, fears, responsibilities and an awareness of her own body. She knows how society may treat her because of her physical difference. Unlike Samsa, she is not discovering the world for the first time. She has survived by confronting its harsh rules for years. Samsa is new to human society; she is already familiar with its indifference and its dangers. The tension between these two experiences gives the story much of its force.

Read side by side, Kafka’s The Metamorphosis and Murakami’s Samsa in Love reveal how deeply the human body can shape identity and social position. Kafka’s Gregor becomes an insect and is gradually treated by his family as something less than human. Murakami’s hunchbacked locksmith is fully human, yet remains socially marked by her body. Samsa, meanwhile, is human in body but cannot yet feel at home inside it. Murakami’s transformation is therefore more than a movement from insect to man. It also questions the divisions we make between normal and abnormal, beautiful and ugly, capable and incapable. The story quietly asks how fair our standards of the human body really are.

In the end, Samsa in Love presents human identity as something unfinished. A person comes to know himself through the body, memory, language, social habits, desire and relationships. Kafka’s Gregor is pushed out of human life and becomes an insect. Murakami’s Samsa moves from an insect-like existence towards humanity and discovers the possibility of crossing the distance between himself and others. Yet this possibility does not arise from a great political transformation, a reunion with his family or a sudden philosophical revelation. It begins with an ordinary encounter—with a young locksmith who has come to repair a lock and, after finishing her work, must return to a dangerous city.

That encounter teaches Samsa that human life is not confined to satisfying hunger or keeping the body safe. The presence of another person, the recognition of difference, the desire for someone and the wish to see that person again are also part of being human. The Samsa who once regarded the human body as weak and inconvenient now wants to live in that body. For within the difficulties of being human there are feelings that no other form of existence could give him. That is the story’s deepest transformation.
